newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn accused of siding with public banks in EU row.
newsitem.headline: Bonn accused of siding with public banks in EU row.

text.p: Germany's private banks on Friday accused the Bonn government of siding with the publicly-owned banks in an increasingly acrimonious dispute over alleged subsidies.

The Federal Association of German Banks, which represents the private banks, said it was convinced the European Union would probe the regional public banks, or Landesbanken, for gaining an unfair advantage by obtaining cheap state funds.
"The federal government has sided with the Landesbanken when its real task is to ensure fair competition," Wolfgang Arnold, the association's deputy general manager, told Reuters.
The Bonn economics ministry was not immediately available for comment.

The dispute centres on a charge filed in 1994 by the private sector banks that 11 billion marks ($6.5 billion) of state capital transferred to publicly-owned regional banks since 1990 constituted a breach of EU subsidy rules.
The public and private banks have failed in a series of talks to reach agreement and banking sources say the row has become increasingly bitter.

Private banking sources said Bonn was so anxious to retain the support of the Landesbanken and savings banks for Europe's planned monetary union that it was exerting subtle pressure on the private banks to drop their complaint with the EU.
Only last week Friedel Neuber, the head of the Federal Association of Public Banks, threatened to withhold support for the single currency if private banks did not withdraw their complaint.
The support of the public banks and myriad savings banks for monetary union is regarded as crucial to persuading Germany's sceptical public to accept giving up the mark.

The banking sources, who spoke on condition of anonymity, alleged Bonn had indirectly threatened the private banks by delaying the approval of a draft law on joint stock firms at a time when calls were growing for limits on bank stakes in industrial firms.
Calls for curbs on bank power grew amid heavy public criticism of the role of private banks in the controversial hostile bid by steelmaker Krupp AG for Thyssen AG in March.
Delaying the law meant that limits on stake ownership may yet be incorporated into the legislation -- a move that could hurt the private banks, the sources said.
In another example of alleged pressure, the Federal Banking Supervisory Authority had increased the capital cost for banks which have bought or plan to buy other banks, the sources said.
That could increase the cost to Deutsche Bank AG and Dresdner Bank AG resulting from the purchase of their respective UK investment banking subsidiaries, Morgan Grenfell and Kleinwort Benson.

Henning Schoppmann, a director of the Federal Association of Public Banks, said relations between Bonn and the private banks were likely to be strained in part because of the role of Deutsche and Dresdner in supporting Krupp's controversial bid.

In addition, Schoppmann said Bonn had been snubbed by the heads of major private banks who failed to show up at a meeting on the dispute on April 14 called by Friedrich Bohl, the chancellery minister.

The Landesbanken are owned by their respective federal states and savings bank associations. They do not offer retail banking but compete with private banks in corporate finance, securities trading and issuing.

In 1990 the federal states started integrating their regional housing development agencies into the regional banks to beef up the banks' weak equity capital before tougher EU rules on capital adequacy came into force in 1993.
The private banks see this as distorting competition because it enabled the regional banks to obtain capital at a price far below what private banks have to pay for capital.
The regional banks see no such distortion.
($ = 1.722 German Marks)
